meta.title: Local Models with Ollama
meta.thesis: Local Models with Ollama is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A developer prototypes a private assistant locally before sending data to hosted models. By the end, they should be able to build or review Ollama local model experiment log with prompt, model, and limits, measure acceptable answer quality on private fixtures, and catch the failure where the local model passes short tests but fails long context examples.

modules.title: Ollama is for local model loops, not fleets
modules.sub: Use it when setup speed and privacy matter more than throughput.
modules.summary: Ollama turns open-weight models into local developer infrastructure.

blocks.title: Local model serving has a different job

spans.text: Problem anchor: a teacher wants a private demo that drafts lesson explanations without sending prompts to a hosted API. Ollama is useful because a learner can pull a model, run it locally, and call a simple HTTP API on localhost.

The KB verdict is clear: Ollama is best for local development, demos, and privacy-sensitive prototypes; it is not the default for high-concurrency production serving with autoscaling, tenant policy, and detailed routing.

blocks.analogy: Ollama is a workbench model server, not a factory loading dock.

spans.text: The worked artifact is a privacy-preserving lesson explainer: the app sends a learner's prompt to an Ollama model on localhost, streams the answer, records first-token and total latency, and refuses to fall back to a cloud model without an explicit operator decision. The failure check is simple: stop the local model and confirm the UI explains the missing local dependency instead of leaking the prompt elsewhere.

options.text: High-concurrency multi-tenant GPU fleets by default.

blocks.title: The model has to exist locally before your app can call it

spans.text: Ollama commands such as pull, run, show, ps, and create manage local model artifacts and active sessions. The local server exposes HTTP endpoints for chat, generate, embeddings, and model management. Streaming JSON is convenient, but clients must parse it deliberately.

blocks.title: A Modelfile is a local model recipe

spans.text: A Modelfile can define the base model, system prompt, prompt template, parameters such as context length, adapters, and license metadata. It gives the local demo a stable contract instead of relying on one-off CLI flags.

blocks.title: Worked Modelfile for a local tutor

spans.text:
FROM llama3.1
PARAMETER num_ctx 8192
SYSTEM You are a concise tutor for agentic AI concepts. Explain with one example and one check question.

Review: num_ctx increases memory use, and the base model license still controls allowed use.

modules.title: Code the local chat smoke test
modules.sub: The smallest app call should check model, latency, and output shape.
modules.summary: A smoke test proves the endpoint works before UI polish.
objectives: Run a local API call shape.
Predict failure when stream handling is wrong.

blocks.title: Ollama local chat smoke test
blocks.code:
import requests, time

payload = {
    "model": "llama3.1",
    "stream": False,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain KV cache in one paragraph."}],
}
start = time.time()
resp = requests.post("http://localhost:11434/api/chat", json=payload, timeout=60)
resp.raise_for_status()
data = resp.json()
latency = time.time() - start

assert "message" in data and "content" in data["message"]
print({"latency_s": round(latency, 2), "preview": data["message"]["content"][:80]})

spans.text: This smoke test disables streaming so the response is easy to assert. A streaming UI can be added after the basic endpoint contract is proven.

predictThenReveal.prompt: What likely breaks if stream stays true but the client still calls resp.json() once?
predictThenReveal.answer: The endpoint can return newline-delimited streaming JSON chunks, so treating the whole response as one JSON object can fail or lose partial-output handling.

spans.text: Checklist: model tag exists locally; service URL is configurable; streaming and non-streaming modes are parsed correctly; latency is logged; prompt data stays local; and the app fails clearly when the model is missing.

modules.title: Know when to graduate beyond Ollama
modules.sub: Local success does not prove production readiness.
modules.summary: Ollama should hand off to gateways or serving runtimes when concurrency, policy, and reliability matter.
objectives: Compare Ollama with vLLM and hosted APIs.

blocks.title: The local demo has honest limits

spans.text: Local performance depends on model size, quantization, VRAM, and offload behavior. Ollama does not automatically provide multi-user auth, budgets, audit logs, autoscaling, or production routing. For many users, move behind a gateway, hosted API, vLLM, or another serving stack.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Use Ollama to learn, prototype, and demo locally; graduate when concurrency, governance, or reliability become requirements.
blocks.useWhen: Use it for offline demos, private prototypes, classroom exercises, and local fallback experiments.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid presenting a laptop-local model as production infrastructure without auth, monitoring, rate limits, evaluation, and license review.

blocks.title: Graduation signal
blocks.prompt: When should an Ollama prototype move to another serving plan?

options.text: As soon as the first local response works.
When multiple users, auth, budgets, high concurrency, or reliability SLAs matter.
Never; local serving is always enough.

blocks.explanation: Production needs more than a localhost endpoint.

gpu.label: GPU
gpu.laymanDefinition: A parallel accelerator for tensor computation.
gpu.technicalNote: For local Ollama use, GPU availability changes the feasible model size, context length, and responsiveness; the lesson treats it as a capacity constraint to measure before promising a workflow.

serving.label: Serving
serving.laymanDefinition: Running a model behind an endpoint so an app can send prompts and receive answers.
serving.technicalNote: Here serving means Ollama's local HTTP API and streaming behavior, not a managed autoscaling fleet; the contract is localhost reachability, model availability, and predictable error handling.

gateway.label: Gateway
gateway.laymanDefinition: The thin layer that decides which model endpoint an app calls.
gateway.technicalNote: In a local-model setup, a gateway should make locality explicit, prevent silent cloud fallback, and surface model-not-found or timeout errors as setup problems.

latency.label: Latency
latency.laymanDefinition: The delay a learner feels before and during the generated answer.
latency.technicalNote: Measure both time to first token and full response time, because local quantized models can feel interactive at short outputs yet stall on long contexts or CPU-only machines.

throughput.label: Throughput
throughput.laymanDefinition: How much local generation work the machine can complete over time.
throughput.technicalNote: For Ollama prototypes, throughput is bounded by local hardware, model size, context length, and concurrent requests; it is a fit check, not just a benchmark number.

versioning.label: Versioning
versioning.laymanDefinition: Recording exactly which local model variant produced a result.
versioning.technicalNote: Ollama tags and model files must be pinned in experiments so a later demo uses the same quantization, prompt behavior, and context assumptions.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: Ollama is designed to run models on a single local machine. Which of the following is a direct consequence of that design?

options.text: It can automatically scale to handle hundreds of simultaneous users.
It cannot serve multiple heavy requests at once without degrading performance.
It requires a cloud account to download model weights.
It replaces the need for a GPU in all cases.

questions.explanation: Because Ollama runs on one machine, it shares that machine's memory and compute across all requests — there's no horizontal scaling, so concurrent heavy load quickly becomes a bottleneck.

questions.prompt: You run `ollama run mistral` and then send a request to the local API. The response comes back as a stream of JSON lines. Your code reads only the very first line and stops. What is the most likely symptom?

options.text: The model crashes and must be restarted with `ollama stop`.
You get a complete response because the first line always contains the full answer.
You receive only a fragment of the generated text and miss the rest of the reply.
The API returns an HTTP 500 error for incomplete reads.

questions.explanation: The local API streams one JSON chunk per line; reading only the first line captures just the opening fragment of the response — you must loop over all lines until the `done` flag is true.

questions.prompt: A Modelfile lets you package defaults for a local model. Which pair of things can you set directly inside a Modelfile?

options.text: A system prompt and the context window size.
A cloud API key and a billing tier.
The number of GPU nodes and a load-balancing strategy.
A Docker registry address and a container restart policy.

questions.explanation: A Modelfile's SYSTEM instruction sets the system prompt and PARAMETER options like `num_ctx` control context length — both are baked in at build time so every run starts with those defaults.

questions.prompt: Name TWO specific gaps that make Ollama a poor fit for a production deployment serving real end-users, and for each gap name one alternative tool or approach that addresses it.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Any two of: (1) No horizontal scaling / single-machine limit → vLLM or a hosted API (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic) can serve many users concurrently. (2) No built-in auth or rate limiting → a hosted API or an API gateway adds those controls. (3) Model memory risk / large VRAM requirement → hosted APIs abstract hardware; vLLM handles multi-GPU sharding. (4) No SLA or uptime guarantee → hosted providers offer SLAs Ollama cannot match.
questions.explanation: Ollama lacks horizontal scaling, access controls, and uptime guarantees — gaps that vLLM (multi-GPU serving) and hosted APIs (managed infrastructure) are specifically built to fill.

questions.prompt: You ask an AI assistant to generate Ollama integration code for you. What is the most important thing to verify before trusting that code in your project?

options.text: That the code uses the latest trendy framework, since AI always picks the best one.
That the streaming loop correctly reads all JSON lines until `done` is true and handles errors.
That the code is fewer than 50 lines, because shorter code is always more correct.
That the model name in the code matches the AI assistant's own model name.

questions.explanation: AI-generated Ollama code most commonly fails by mishandling the streaming response — a correct smoke test checks that every chunk is consumed and that network or parse errors are caught.
